subtopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REASSESSMENT OF DESIGN

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraiih (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REASSESSMENT OF DESIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a brief statement to make concerning the Northumberland strait crossing.
The department has completed the review of the tenders submitted for the first section of the Northumberland crossing. These tenders covered the construction of approximately two miles of causeway, extending from the New Brunswick shore and in a relatively shallow section of the crossing.
All tenders have been carefully analysed. The prices quoted on particular components such as the concrete structure and durable rock are very much higher than anticipated. This wide gap between the estimates and the quotations received indicates that the whole project, as originally designed, would cost a great deal more than anticipated.
For this reason the government has decided not to accept any of the tenders submitted and to reassess the design of the project. One factor adding heavily to the cost of the present design is the inclusion of rails on the crossing. The design of a crossing combining causeway, bridge and tunnel sections was largely determined by the desire to provide both highway and rail transportation on the nine mile link between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. Such a design could be greatly simplified by leaving rails off the crossing and continuing to provide rail service by ferry.
With the elimination of rail service all elements of the crossing could be changed. For example, on the causeway portion it will be desirable to re-examine the width, the crest elevation, and the need for the concrete superstructure originally contemplated.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
On the bridge portion the double deck structure designed to carry the two modes of transportation would no longer be required. The reduced loading in providing for highway traffic only permits consideration of longer
spans and fewer pier elements. The design to provide for marine traffic through the crossing would be affected not only because of simplified requirements, but also because of the removal of the controlling railway grades. With freedom to work to the higher permissible highway grades, consideration could be given to a high level bridge section for total free navigation, a review of the tunnel proposal with revised grades and ventilation requirements, and a short high level highway bridge over a lock. These reviews of design will affect the costs of both bridges and causeway and will permit a reassessment of the desirable lengths of each type of structure relative to the varying depths of water.
Before taking the decision not to accept the tenders submitted, the Minister of Transport and I met with Premier Campbell of Prince Edward Island and explained to him the considerations involved in this decision. At his request the government has agreed, in its reassessment of design, to examine whether a simplified method of including rails on the crossing would be practicable. It was made clear to the premier that whether or not a decision was finally made to provide rails on the crossing, the government of Canada recognizes that there is an obligation to provide efficient rail service to Prince Edward Island so long as there is any effective demand for such service, and the government has every intention of carrying out that obligation, regardless of the method by which rail cars are transported from the island to the mainland.
Even if a tender award were made now on the basis of bids received for the New Brunswick causeway section, by the time mobilization and preparation of the quarries were completed the progress on actual crossing construction during the 1967 construction season may be more than offset by the improved rate of production in subsequent years consequent on a simplified design. While it is anticipated that the redesign will take several months, this will not necessarily delay completion of the project.
I would like to conclude by reasserting the government's intention to continue with this project. I might add that the causeway approach road on Prince Edward Island will

Prince Edward Island Causeway soon be completed, and tenders for construction of a highway interchange at Albany, P.E.I., are expected to be called this summer.

subtopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REASSESSMENT OF DESIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Prince Edward Island will learn of the minister's statement with some apprehension. Although the minister has expressed some hope that the final completion date might still be met, there will be some delay. There is some consolation, of course, in the minister's avowed determination to keep on with the construction of this very important work, because there has been a fear that the project might be dropped entirely.
The possible elimination of rail service from this causeway would have a very important economic effect on Prince Edward Island. I am somewhat assured by the government's recognition of its obligation to continue to provide suitable rail service to Prince Edward Island by one means or another. I hope, along with Premier Campbell, that even yet some feasible way of including rail service on the causeway might be found.
There will be an onus on the government to keep the people of Prince Edward Island, of New Brunswick and indeed the people of Canada advised as fully as possible on the progress of this very important project. We are disappointed, of course, that the construction which it was anticipated would take place this year will not in fact take place. There is considerable cause for worry because of the wide gap between the estimates of costs and the quotations received. We have no guarantee that this will not continue to be the case, regardless of what the new design will be. We would like to be assured that in future estimates of costs will be as accurate as it is possible to make them.
Since I had but very brief advance information with regard to this matter, through no fault of the minister, I think I have nothing more to say at this time. But in the near future, perhaps even today, we might have some questions to ask the minister to further clarify the situation, especially with regard to the submission of Mr. McCulloch to the Department of Public Works and other matters.

subtopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REASSESSMENT OF DESIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this matter is of sufficient importance to the people of Prince Edward Island in particular and the people of Canada in general that very soon the minister ought to call the estimates of the Department of Public Works in order that

the house may have an opportunity to ascertain all the facts and have some discussion of this question.
The primary purpose in building a causeway was to enable the people of Prince Edward Island to eliminate the ferrying of rail traffic and to bring out their goods directly. The building of a causeway without adequate rail facilities in my opinion is not going to solve the problem which faces the people of Prince Edward Island. There has been some suggestion of a good deal of incompetence which resulted in the gap between the estimates of the department for the project and the bids quoted by the various construction firms. The department can be out a small percentage in its estimates but it ought not to be as far out as the minister seems to indicate.
I think for this reason the whole matter ought to be reviewed. To go to the expense of building a causeway without providing adequate rail facilities on that causeway is to do only half the job. I think the House of Commons should have an opportunity to discuss this matter before the government commits itself any further.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the last three years the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I and others in our party have attempted to obtain some declaration from the government on the establishment of straight base lines for the protection of our territorial sea and fishing zones. We have had no success. The purpose of the bill is to establish by law instead of by negotiations straight base lines for the British Columbia coasts enclosing and including Queen Charlotte sound, Hecate strait and Dixon entrance. This will permit the parliament of Canada to have a say in the location in our territorial sea and fishing zones and will prevent the government from selling us out.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Chairman, I apologize for making it possible for the minister to leave the house. Perhaps she is tired of hearing me speak for the third time in three days.
I assure her and my colleagues that I am not going to make a habit of this. I think even the minister would have to acknowledge that the amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act that are placed before us in this bill are mere patchwork, in spite of the fact that a new citizenship act was heralded by announcements in four throne speeches from 1963 to 1967. The end product clearly shows the uncertainty which surrounds its origins and the difficulties this particular bill is having in joining the legislative list.
I want to assure the minister that, speaking for the official opposition, in spite of one or two comments and criticisms we welcome the concept of the bill and are glad that its passage has been given priority during centennial year. I assure the minister that nothing will be placed in the way of the swift enactment of the bill. I should just like to list quickly four of five complaints, so to speak, or comments and perhaps the minister will have some suggestions to make about them when she closes the debate.
The first and most serious is that the court of citizenship appeal, that is the Exchequer Court, unlike the immigration appeal court will sit ahead of or prior to the final grant of discretion by the minister. It is only a matter of months ago that we were dealing with the Immigration Act, and the process of appeal from the Immigration Act of a few months ago to the citizenship act has been reversed.
It seems to me, in any event, that this is a contradiction in policy and I think parliament and the country are entitled to an explanation for this shift in policy. After all, immigration appeals in matters involving security-and we had quite a helpful debate on this point -are left to the minister. I think there should be frankness in the matter of security
[Mr. Enns.1

cases and the granting of citizenship, particularly in so far as that grant concerns alleged members of the communist party. It seems to me that there is a paradox wherein the party itself is legal in Canada, but early membership in that party may rule out, even if there are not other reasons for so doing, the award of citizenship. I have always felt that the democratic fabric of this country was strong enough to withstand this type of assault, if it is an assault; or to put it another way, I have always felt we should not be so uncertain about our fabric that this paradoxical situation should become enmeshed in our law.
I have heard a certain anecdote many times, and I am sure the minister has also, about the former president Clemenceau of France. Some advisers and friends approached him and said to him: "Monsieur le president, your son is a communist." The great president then said to them: "But my son is 21. Come to me when he is 31 with the same story and I will begin to worry." I do not want anything more to be read into this anecdote than what I imply by it, but I think that with the experience in North America since the days of McCarthy we have seen what early membership in either the so-called communist party or in groups espousing its objectives might mean to a man's future.
The hon. member for Carleton, (Mr. Bell) in a most compelling speech in the private members hour last Friday, spoke of the anomaly of children of diplomats and service people. I hope the minister will be able to clear up that point when she comments on this act.
Then I want to make mention of the revocation of citizenship. I am one who believes that revocation should not be a matter of ministerial or regulatory discretion, but should be part and parcel of an actual conviction. Perhaps the minister, who is a distinguished counsel, would like to comment on this problem.
Then I think it will be admitted, as it has been to some of us by the members of the minister's own department, that it is time we had a revision and consolidation of the regulations outlining the qualifications for citizenship. I have particularly in mind the people who came before 1930, and then the group which came in the period between 1930 and 1947, and so on. My information from the minister's own department is that the only body of law, if a confidential memorandum is a body of law, is a series of these documents.

Mr. Chairman, it is my desire to take advantage of the discussion on clause
Canadian Citizenship Act 1 of the bill to add my voice in discussing one phase of the government's policy which has been followed persistently over the years, and in this bill I see that no change in policy is proposed. A visitor coming to Canada can do so on a temporary basis on a tourist visa. The only other way one can be admitted to Canada is as a landed immigrant. Such a person to arrive here as a landed immigrant must be absolutely acceptable to the officials of the department and to the government. Once the landed immigrant is here he must remain in this country for a period of five years before he can apply to a citizenship court for the privilege of being granted Canadian citizenship. If the court is of the opinion that he will make a good citizen and is in favour of granting him Canadian citizenship, the application of the immigrant then goes to the citizenship branch of the department where the final decision is made by the minister.
What has been our experience over the years? I have heard of several cases of landed immigrants receiving favourable decisions from the citizenship court, but being refused the right of citizenship by the department in Ottawa. This is serious enough, but what is more serious is that in handing down the ministerial decision no reason is given to the landed immigrant, who has been here five years and has received favourable recommendation from the court, as to why the minister has turned down his application. He does not know what is held against him and what the charge is. It may be based on misrepresentation and lies, but since he does not know it he cannot contest it.
It is not sufficient for a court to recommend the granting of citizenship. In my own constituency there are immigrants who have been here for five years and who have received a favourable judgment from the court, but who were then turned down by the minister, with no reason given. Two years later they went back before the court, once again received a favourable recommendation and again were turned down by the minister. No reason is given. They do not know why they are denied citizenship. So, what happens? After they are turned down twice, and very often after they are turned down once, I know what they do in Vancouver East. They get in touch with their member of parliament. They ask: What have I done wrong; what is held against me?

I take the matter up with the minister of citizenship. What answer does a member of

Canadian Citizenship Act the House of Commons receive? He receives the same answer as that given to the applicant for Canadian citizenship: We are sorry, Mr. Winch, but we cannot tell you the reason; we will not give you any reason. Here we have one who is attempting to get Canadian citizenship. He has been admitted to Canada because the department of immigration thought he would make a good citizen. He has been a good citizen for nine years and in that time has been twice recommended for citizenship by the courts. Then, the minister not only has the power but uses the power to say to the applicant and to the member of parliament: We will not tell you why the applicant has been refused.
I have had the experience of following through these citizenship and immigration cases, when I have received these answers. Upon more than one occasion I have found that the reason the department refused the applicant was the result of lies and charges laid by somebody who was jealous of that individual, envious of him for some reason, and wanted to do something to hurt him. How are these applicants for citizenship, in all justice and fairness, going to be able to do something about it? I do know that in clause 30 of this amending bill there is provision for the right of appeal when one is turned down by the court. On the other hand, there is nothing in the bill that I can see whereby one who is favourably recommended by the court can appeal against the minister's decision, and know what the charge is.
Now, Mr. Chairman, surely this is about the most dictatorial, unjust policy that could ever be conceived in a democratic country or in a country of justice. This is a situation which, I will admit, completely burns me up, the principle is so unfair and unjust. I do not believe it is right in any Canadian policy or in any aspect of our life that a person should be found guilty without knowing what the charge is, and without being given the right to defend himself.
I do regret exceedingly that this change is not in the bill. I realize the minister has only had responsibility for citizenship for a short time. However, I appeal to her in the name of justice, in the name of fairness, that if she is going to take the ministerial power to deny citizenship to those recommended by the courts, in the name of decency let the individual or his representative in parliament know what the charge is, so it can be met.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly in support of the bill before us.

I feel it deserves the support of all the members of the house, since it expands the proud concept of Canadian citizenship. It may be that this bill could have been dealt with in earlier sessions of this house. However I can think of no more suitable, no more fitting time to deal with a bill of this sort than in the centennial session of the Canadian parliament.
I believe a very useful amendment to the citizenship act is the one permitting older people who have lived their lives here, but who may not have had an opportunity to acquire a detailed knowledge of French or English, to acquire Canadian citizenship upon demonstration of having been here for an extended period; thereby demonstrating the real test of citizenship that living lives as good citizens, raising families and contributing to the development of the country.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, when the minister concludes this debate if she would give some further assurance with respect to the amendments before us dealing with section 12 of the citizenship act, the taking of the formal oath for Canadian citizenship. Many of us recall that about a year ago a problem arose when a family from a European country felt their religious conscience was such that they preferred to affirm rather than take an oath. The citizenship court judge in question felt he did not have the power to allow them to do so. I am somewhat concerned that it is not clearly spelled out in the act that people who, through the dictates of their conscience, feel they can only affirm rather than swear the usual oath will be entitled to do so. I hope the minister will give some explanation and reassurance upon this important point.
I suggest that the minister should be commended because of the amendments in the bill before us removing what, in effect, are the remaining distinctions between natural born and naturalized Canadian citizens. I think it is proven almost daily throughout the country that good citizenship does not flow automatically from the accident of birth. There is a lot to be said for the value placed upon citizenship by those immigrants coming to this country after having made a definite choice of Canada as the place in which they want to live and want their descendents to live for generations onward.
The removal of this distinction, Mr. Chairman, I believe helps to strengthen the concept and value of Canadian citizenship.
May 31, 1967,	COMMONS
Another improvement is brought forward throught the creation of an appeal procedure to deal with the decisions of citizenship court judges. I believe this provision fills one of the greatest gaps in the existing citizenship law.
I found it rather strange, Mr. Chairman, that there were appeals for such things as careless driving or throwing cigarette wrappers on the sidewalk, but no appeal from the decision of a judge on the vital question of whether or not a person could be a citizen of this country. I always felt it was certainly an anomaly to leave to the discretion of the individual citizenship court judges across the country exactly what criteria they would use, the questions they would ask and the manner in which they would come to a decision on whether the person appearing before them demonstrated in the course of the hearing that he ought to be given Canadian citizenship.
In the past there were judges, and I have heard it said there are still judges, who applied some very odd standards in arriving at their decisions as to whether or not the applicant should be recommended for Canadian citizenship. I have heard it said, and I have seen evidence of this myself in the past although not at the present time in our own area, that questions are asked in a narrow and discriminatory manner. It is obvious that simply knowing the name of the largest river in Canada for example does not constitute the supreme test of someone's ability to be a good Canadian citizen. It seems to me that the real test is the desire of the person to link his life fully and completely with this country, its present and its future. I think that without requiring a detailed examination of someone's knowledge of our history, geography or form of government, it should be possible, through questioning the prospective applicant about the life he leads in this country, his job, his hopes and his intention for the future, to determine whether or not the person in question really is one we want to have as a Canadian citizen.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Chairman, that a knowledge of our history, geography and form of government is not useful. Certainly it is. However, it is equally useful to a natural born citizen. It is rather strange that because a person is born here he can know nothing whatever about our history, our geography or form of government and still be considered a citizen in the fullest sense of the term.

This takes almost all their energy. We should certainly not expect applicants to know more than other Canadian citizens. I think they should know as much, but not more.
I dare the parliamentary secretary to address these questions to a group of a hundred citizens chosen indiscriminately. I think he will find that not many people know the answers. I believe some common sense should be used.
As one hon. member has reminded us, one has established a certain vested right in being a landed immigrant. He cannot be thrown out of the country without good cause. At the same time, citizenship is withheld from him. This it seems to me has created a curious situation. Let us have either one or the other. If we say to a landed immigrant who has been here, say, ten years "You have a vested right to stay here", while at the same time withholding citizenship from him, we are surely acting in an illogical manner. They would like to be part of these festivities, and I can think of no better way of including them than to accord citizenship in the manner I have proposed.
I should like the minister and the parliamentary secretary to give serious consideration to this idea. If the cabinet would introduce an amendment along these lines, and if the house would approve it, so much the better.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RESIDENCE REQUIREMENTS, APPEAL COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, citizenship and amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act have been the subject of discussion in every parliament since I came here in 1962. Members of all parties, including backbench government members, who represent constituencies which have fairly heavy ethnic representation, have bombarded the government with suggestions for improvements to the Canadian Citizenship Act and its day to day implementation. They have made suggestions which would wipe out the anomalies that have existed and still exist.
I was amazed that the minister brought forward what another hon. member has referred to as a patchwork bill instead of placing before us the major redrafting that we have been promised for three or four years. This is a bill which will make relatively minor improvements to the act under which we operate. I am also amazed that the minister did not make an opening statement, explaining the purposes of this bill and what she hopes its passage will accomplish, indicating


also when we may expect to get the major revision promised by successive ministers.
When he opened the debate on behalf of the official opposition the hon. member for Royal hoped that the minister would answer questions at the end of the debate. I have no objection to the parliamentary secretary doing that, but on such an important bill and such an important subject I think the house and the country should have heard some opening remarks by the minister to indicate the purposes of the bill.
It is all very well for the hon. member for York East to say, as he did in a pretty eloquent speech, that this bill goes a long way toward wiping out the differences in respect to citizenship between people born in Canada and people who come to Canada. I do not think the bill goes that far. The hon. member for York East pointed out that people who come to this country and apply for citizenship must be able to answer a large number of questions, which he said most citizens could not answer. I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that without some study a majority of the members of parliament might have difficulty passing the citizenship examination, if it were necessary for them to pass it in order to become citizens, or even to become members of parliament.
Those who were fortunate enough to be born in Canada do not have to pass any examination to get citizenship.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RESIDENCE REQUIREMENTS, APPEAL COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Why should we?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RESIDENCE REQUIREMENTS, APPEAL COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think we should; but I am not convinced that a person who comes to this country, stays here five years, supports himself and his family, sends his children to school, pays taxes and all other expenses, should have to pass a citizenship examination.
However, that is not the main point on which I rose to speak. I rose to say that, as with so many things that parliament and government do, this bill is mere window dressing. Under some of its provisions we are making promises and commitments to people wishing to become citizens, but under other clauses we are going back on those promises and commitments.
Clause 31 provides that when a citizenship court has held a hearing and decides that a person is qualified to become a citizen, the minister may grant him citizenship. That word "may" is not in the clause by accident. While the minister may grant that person citizenship, I presume the minister may also not grant him citizenship. This is a pretty
May 31, 1967

sweeping power to give the minister. As has happened so often in the past, when the minister refuses to grant citizenship, he will not tell the applicant, his lawyer, or even his member of parliament the reason for the refusal.
I am not going to name names today, but a former minister of immigration, now Minister of Labour, who was in his seat a few moments ago, knows one case which I have in mind. In many parts of Canada very distinguished people have been refused citizenship. I can think of a distinguished professor in the city of Toronto, a world famous authority in his own field, a landed immigrant who has held many important positions in government service, and he has been consistently unable to get citizenship. I can think of a professor in a Canadian medical college who came to this country from the United States as a landed immigrant. He is a brilliant scientist, and under his direction his medical department expanded tenfold or more. He was able to attract to it many distinguished people from other countries. He has represented Canada at a large number of world scientific conferences to which he was sent by his university, and I suppose on occasion by the Canadian government. But that man, despite the most distinguished sponsors, including a deputy minister in the federal service, was repeatedly turned down for citizenship.
The hon. member for Royal questioned whether a person should be refused citizenship because of his political views. I doubt whether the two people I have mentioned were ever members of the communist party. But even if they were at one time, if they are of a calibre and character which permits the government of Canada to allow them to come to Canada, to live permanently in it, and to occupy important and distinguished positions, then what earthly common sense is there in refusing them citizenship? If a person is a security risk or is involved in espionage, then there might be a reason; no doubt there is. But because a person disagrees with the foreign policy of the United States, disagrees with the foreign policy of Canada, or thinks that Canada should not have nuclear bombs, are these sufficient reasons to refuse to grant him citizenship? When we do that we take away the democratic rights which all of us like to believe every person in Canada has. I suggest to the government that it is time we wiped out this type of thing.
Canadian Citizenship Act [DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I should like to talk about another matter. As I have said before, and as I say now, in my constituency there are a number of persons whose applications for citizenship have been turned down over a long period. These are people I suppose who came here in the early 1900's after world war I, who were sympathizers with the communist revolution in Russia. Some of them I suppose belonged to the communist party. Others never belonged to the communist party itself but belonged to what those of us who have fought communism or have had anything to do with it refer to as front organizations, those fraternal organizations and co-operatives which, I admit, were established by the communist party and its sympathizers.
These people do not come to me. Not a single person has come to me to ask for my help in obtaining citizenship. Perhaps this is because my record of antagonism to communism in Canada or in any other country is so well known. These are people, however, who have been in Canada for 10, 15, 25 or 30 years. Surely it makes no sense that they should be denied citizenship after all these years simply because they belonged to the communist party or to one of the fraternal organizations, the names of which I will not burden you with at this time. Even more serious is the fact that, not only are they denied citizenship but they are not given the reasons for the denial of citizenship, nor are they given the opportunity to present evidence to show that a mistake has been made, if one has been made.
This certainly is not the place to discuss the R.C.M.P. I have not been quiet about the fact that I am not the greatest admirer in this house of the R.C.M.P. and its ability to decide who is or is not subversive. Even if one should be the greatest admirer of the R.C.M.P., he must face up to the fact that it is composed of a group of human beings who, like any other groups of human beings, or like any other individual, can and do make mistakes. I shall not go over the record, but we did have a case, the name of which I cannot remember at the moment, which my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, raised some years ago concerning the young man who was refused the right to re-enlist in the navy because, supposedly, his uncle was an official of the communist party. When my colleague took up the matter and investigated it, it was found that although they had the same name there was no relationship. If my colleague had not
May 31, 1967

Canadian Citizenship Act taken the matter up and looked into it, that young man never would have known the reason he was refused the right to re-enlist in the navy.
My colleague, the hon. member for Springfield, says, "Suppose it was his uncle". We have come a long way. Surely we are not going to convict people or say they are guilty because of association, especially when the association is within a family. We choose our friends, but we do not have much to do about choosing our families. What I am saying is, having come a long way in our efforts to meet the difficulties in respect of prospective immigrants, surely we can devise a procedure whereby people who are denied citizenship because allegedly they do not meet the security standards, whatever they are-and I as a member of parliament do not know what they are; perhaps the parliamentary secretary knows-can be given a general idea of what they are accused of. I am not saying at this time that this should be done in open court. I am not saying that the person who makes the accusation should appear before the court. I am not saying that the specific details must be documented. I recognize the tremendous difficulties we face when we try to deal with the whole question of security.
I do not believe it would be impossible to have an appeal board composed of distinguished citizens whose records are so clearly favourable that they could be given, in confidence if necessary, a general statement of the reasons a person is being turned down. This board would be in a position to set the record straight, if the record obtained by the government agencies involved should be incorrect. There is nothing in this bill which spells out that right. There is nothing in it which spells out the right of a person whose application for citizenship has been turned down to be given a bill of particulars or even general knowledge concerning the particulars, so that he can answer the charges or explain the charges in order to clear his name. It seems to me that this is completely contrary to every principle of justice, democracy, or human rights which we in this country repeatedly espouse.
While it is not my intention to vote against the bill, we have some reservations and may move some amendments. I do say, however, that for me, and I believe other members of this house who have spoken on this subject on a number of occasions, it is a bitter disappointment that the government has not really met any of the specific objections which repeatedly over the years have been made by

members of parliament on both sides of the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am particularly happy to participate in the discussion of this bill because it heralds the removal of discrimination against Canadians not bom in Canada and, as well, makes the act more meaningful. When we speak of our natural resources seldom do we fail to boast of our vast mineral deposits, our vast forests and the abundance of hydro power, to say nothing of the great deposits of oil, gas and so on. But how often do we mention the more important prerequisites for the development of a modern industrial society: our manpower and the concept of unity, with a single concept of citizenship.
I recall that in February, 1959 the present Minister of Transport, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, introduced a bill in this house which was designed to remove the discriminatory section of the act-which also is the objective of this bill-whereby a naturalized Canadian citizen, under certain circumstances, is subject to the loss of his citizenship. However, like many other good moves advanced by private members, it was talked out by the supporters of the Conservative party.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
This day and age shows unmistakable trends toward a lessening of narrow nationalism, more particularly because the present act is in conflict with the spirit and letter of the Canadian Bill of Rights, which was supported unanimously in this house. I am referring to the section of the act which provides that under certain circumstances a naturalized Canadian citizen can still have his Canadian citizenship papers revoked by the governor in council. I have been advocating, ever since I was elected to this house in 1958, the elimination of discrimination against naturalized Canadian citizens so that henceforth they will stand on an equal footing with the natural born citizen. I submit that if a naturalized Canadian citizen should commit an offence of a treasonable nature the law will take care of him, the same law that would apply to a natural born Canadian citizen.
I have always felt strongly about the need to eliminate this discrimination, not just because I happen to be a naturalized Canadian citizen but there are thousands in the same category, all of whom by accepting Canadian citizenship have accepted all the duties and obligations that go with it. I cannot see any difference between the duties and obligations
May 31, 1967

imposed upon them as citizens and those imposed on persons born in Canada. I submit that we have a Canadian citizenship of sorts; however, it lacks a cohesive force. Our Fathers of Confederation believed they could accomplish the building of a nation with two ethnic stocks, the French and the English. Little thought was then given to the introduction of many other ethnic stocks. We are built on the bedrock of a bicultural state, but the superstructure also includes a large number of other racial groups. Therefore I am pleased that in the interest of Canada the perpetuation of second-class citizenship will, by the passing of this bill, be eliminated. This will help to unify the racial groups in this nation where unity is the essence of successful development.
Fourteen years ago Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, addressing a gathering in the city of Toronto, had this to say:
I believe it is because we have learned to respect one another and to conserve our heritage that it has been possible since the war to admit 800,000 immigrants into our country without disrupting or even disturbing the basic character of our national life. These men, women and children are making a real contribution to our national life. Without them, we would be the poorer economically, culturally and spiritually.
Most of them have come to Canada with the firm intention of becoming good Canadian citizens, and we are making it possible for them to develop a genuine attachment to this country, because of the increasing respect and understanding we have learned to have for the traditions and backgrounds of one another.
In November, 1962, I moved the first reading of Bill C-88, an act to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act. The purpose of the bill was to enable a citizenship court to recommend the granting of a certificate of citizenship to an applicant who is the wife of a Canadian citizen, even though she is unable to speak either the English or French language.
There are several hundred wives of Canadian citizens who by reason of age or because they are living in isolated places have not been able to master the English or the French languages, and indeed are unlikely to ever learn them sufficiently to qualify for citizenship when they appear before a judge for examination. Some of them can carry on a conversation in more or less broken English and can understand basic questions put to them-this also applies to many of the male applicants-but when they are in the court, facing the usually stern countenance of a robed judge, they become panicky and tongue-tied and fail to pass the examination. As a result, they are rejected.
805
Canadian Citizenship Act
They are advised to reapply after an additional period of two years, and when they do they have to again pay a $10 fee to go through the same process, with possibly the same result. This routine has discouraged many rejected applicants from reapplying and has thus prevented their becoming legal citizens of the country of their adoption. The entire system of examination requires revision.
Applicants for citizenship are asked questions by the court, some of which could stump even a member of parliament, as was pointed out by my good friend the hon. member for York East. Let me give you some examples of what I mean. The hon. member for York East gave some examples. In a list of 42 questions asked by a judge of applicants for citizenship the following appeared: How are members of the Senate appointed? Do you know what year Jacques Cartier landed in Canada? Can you name the two leaders of the 1837 rebellion? How did Canada become a country as a result of an agreement between certain provinces? What is the name of this act of parliament? What are the names of the provinces that joined in this federation? How many territories are there in Canada? What is the largest province in area? What province has the largest population? What is the name of the most recent act of parliament affecting our constitution? Which level of government is responsible for building highways? Which province produces most lumber?
Just imagine, Mr. Chairman.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RESIDENCE REQUIREMENTS, APPEAL COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RESIDENCE REQUIREMENTS, APPEAL COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
These are samples of questions put by some of our citizenship courts to immigrants seeking to become Canadian citizens. It seems to me we can devise a better and more simple set of questions for those newcomers who are anxious to become citizens. In October, 1961, a delegation from the Canadian Council of National Groups met in Ottawa and presented a brief to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration seeking a revision of the Canadian Citizenship Act, which at present denies citizenship for various reasons, none of which have been made clear to the applicant. In this regard I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I honestly believe that applicants for citizenship who were rejected for reasons other than the lack of language requirements, should be given an opportunity to present a defence against accusations in which, in many
May 31. 1967

Canadian Citizenship Act cases, petty jealousies and animosities were involved. Their cases should be reviewed by the minister, and I urge the government to do something about this form of discrimination.
For several years the citizenship branch has been more or less neglected. However, since it has been divorced from immigration-and here I must say that I do not know whether this is for the best-we should look forward to some improvement, and we hope it will receive the attention which its importance to the development of the nation warrants.
There is a definite need for more counseling of immigrants whose contacts with the Canadian community should be encouraged and fostered.
In large centres such as Toronto, Montreal, Hamilton, Windsor and the lakehead, where perhaps 50 per cent of all post-war immigrants are concentrated, the establishment of citizenship offices would be justified. If we are to meet the problem of integration, which is a continuing problem, then the expense of establishing these offices is more than justified.
Such an office could serve as an information service for newcomers. It would recruit a large group of volunteer workers who would assist with reception, translation, the teaching of the English language and any other service required by immigrants.
In addition to the usual services performed by a citizenship office, there could be a close liaison with the local department of manpower on matters of discrimination in employment and housing. Many immigrants and members of minority groups encounter problems in the area of civic rights, yet few persons know that the local manpower office deals with complaints of this kind. They would more readily go to a citizenship office in connection with economic, social and cultural rights. These offices would provide a uniformity of services throughout Canada.
At the present time many of the national groups or individuals offer assistance to members of their own nationality. This type of assistance could be very helpful if channelled through a citizenship office. Presently this assistance is not on a professional or organized basis, and since it is offered by persons of the same nationality it can deter or retard integration. Then also, there are some ethnic group leaders who claim political control of groups, and this is a dangerous and unhealthy condition which leads to political exploitation.
I am convinced that if we gave more attention to problems of citizenship on a local level we would remove some of the criticisms
[Mr. Badanai.l
which were heard during the hearings of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bi-culturalism. The citizenship office would be able to deal with a problem before it developed into a national issue.
I believe that integration is the basis of Canadian unity and that all groups and individuals are bound together in a common citizenship and contribute to the development of a common heritage. This is not window dressing, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North.
I wish to congratulate the minister upon bringing forward this particular measure, which will eliminate a long standing discrimination that has irritated newcomers for a long time. I may add that personally I am particularly appreciative of the citizenship judge, Mayor Ernest Reed, who during the time he has been president of the citizenship court at Fort William, has served the whole district of Thunder Bay from White River in the east to Atikokan in northwestern Ontario. He has shown great tact and consideration in the examination of applicants for citizenship. If we had more men of his calibre in every city in Canada, there would be no criticism of the citizenship examination procedure in Canada. I am proud of the fact that I had the privilege and the pleasure of recommending him for the office which he fills with efficiency and dignity.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROGRAM OF INTERNSHIP IN LEGISLATIVE PROCESSES

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Hales (Wellington South) moved:
subtopic: SUGGESTED PROGRAM OF INTERNSHIP IN LEGISLATIVE PROCESSES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of establishing a form of internship program in the House of Commons; the purpose of the said program being to better equip outstanding young political scientists, .iournalists and law school faculty members, with a better understanding of the national legislative process; the participants to be brought to Ottawa for six to nine months of fulltime work as assistants to members of the House of Commons and to be paid a minimum stipend financed by the government and an established foundation grant, competition for the fellowship to be made each year, announced to coincide with the opening of a session.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of bringing this subject once again before the house in the form of a resolution. Last June 27, I had an opportunity to speak on this resolution at some length. I do not propose to take the time of the house today to repeat what I said at that time but will simply make a few brief introductory remarks. The resolution was conceived in my mind because of the great accumulation of briefs, reading material, bills, and other research work which many members of this house have to undertake.
As our government increases in complexity, it is becoming more apparent that a member is in need of help in one form or another. One of the best ways in which the individual member may secure this assistance would be I believe by the adoption of an internship for students of political science, journalism and law. They would come to Ottawa under a
May 31. 1967

Suggested Internship Program program of internship similar to that of the medical student who serves his internship in a hospital before he starts to practice. I can think of no better place than parliament hill to obtain the experience, the practical knowledge, which people in these professions should have. This is the background of the concept of this resolution.
What is the answer to the problem? We have assistance available in the library. This scheme has been in operation for about two years, and I believe the staff has been brought up to about ten research people. They have two secretaries. It is estimated that the cost of the staff for this year will be about $115,000, according to the estimates. In his report the librarian has stated that only 68 members have used this service. It would appear from the lack of use of this service it is not providing the type of help for which the member is looking.
We must, therefore, turn to another field and I believe that field is the internship program which I am promoting in this resolution I believe that in order to keep my remarks in some sequence I should, first of all, briefly set out the purpose of the resolution, the method of selecting the interns and the source of the funds that would be required to pay for the program. Then, perhaps I could quote from one or two of the editorials that appeared the last time this internship resolution was discussed.
I think I have said enough about the purpose of the resolution. We all realize the purpose and the need for the program. What about the method of selection? How would these interns be chosen? These are proposals I am putting forward and I hope we will be able to go into the details at some other time or place. The intern would be selected through a nationwide competition. I believe the age of these people should be from 21 to 25 years. The criteria for selection would be superior training, practical experience and professional competence.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I suggest that a committee be made up of two Conservatives two Liberals, one member of the New Democratic party, one from the Social Credit party, two political scientists, two lawyers and two journalists, and they would pick those who are suitable for an internship. The applications would be made by the graduates in the three categories I have mentioned. These applications would be received in December and a selection made

by March 31 so that the interns could commence work on September 1.
There are many other details I could go into, such as how much they should be paid and that sort of thing, but I do not want to take up too much time because many others may want to speak on the resolution.
All of this costs money, Mr. Speaker. It has been suggested that we pay these interns a living wage similar to that paid medical interns-something in the neighbourhood of $4,500 or $5,000 a year. I think the government would be well advised to consider setting up a centennial fund of $1 million for this purpose. If this amount was invested at 6 per cent, say, for easy figuring, and we paid the interns $4,500 a year the fund would take care of about 12 interns. We could also turn to organizations such as the Ford Foundation, who I am sure would be interested in contributing to an internship scheme such as that outlined in this resolution.
I am sure that the funds would be forthcoming, Mr. Speaker. This type of internship program has been in operation in the United States for a number of years and has worked very successfully. It would provide personal assistance to the member which at the moment we do not have. Naturally, those employed in the library must work on a nonpartisan basis, but I think members would prefer to supervise their own research work rather than rely on impartial, broadly based material prepared by an independent staff. I think each member would benefit from better research and would be able personally to supervise the work of his assistant.
I can think of many jobs that these interns could do while working with a member of parliament. They could, for example, prepare research material, get material ready for speeches, read over many of the briefs that come to members, and best of all assist members with very complicated legislation coming before the house. I do not think there is a member in the house who would not admit that he comes into this chamber ill-prepared to study and digest legislation and to make really clear and concise remarks about it.
In this regard one has only to cast his mind back to the Canada Pension Plan, which came before this chamber. What time and what facilities had each one of us to study that piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker? I think of the great transportation bill that came before the house last session and also the unification bill. I am sure that all of us could have used

May 31, 1967	COMMONS
to great advantage the help of an intern in these particular fields.
Think also, Mr. Speaker, of the great training this scheme would give a person who won an internship. Look at the great value the experience would be to him. If he returned to practice law he would be a better lawyer. If he went into the field of journalism he would be a much better journalist. If he became a professor in political science, think how much more capable he would be in the classroom.
Another consideration is that many of these young interns may have in the back of their minds the thought that some day they would like to be a member of parliament. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, just how much better members they would be having had this internship and having had the opportunity of being here for at least one term. I do not think I need dwell any longer on what a great help they would be to the members of this house; indeed their appointment would be to the mutual advantage of both members and interns.
I should like to conclude my brief introduction to this resolution, Mr. Speaker, by putting on the record one or two extracts from editorials that appeared after I introduced this resolution on June 27, 1966, during our last session. There is this paragraph in an editorial which appeared in the London Free Press on July 4, 1966:
It is a plan that merits consideration in that it would serve a dual purpose. The hon. member who has presented this resolution is to be commended for bringing it to the attention of the house and therefore to the Canadian public. If there is any criticism to be made of his proposal it is that it does not go far enough. By that I do not mean that there is not room in our parliamentary system for what the hon. member sets out in his proposal. If the hon. member's proposal were adopted I hope it would not be thought that there is not room for what I might call a general system for providing administrative assistants for members of parliament.
The hon. member said that in the United States Congress and Senate there is an internship program of the sort he proposes. That is quite true. However, in addition to interns
May 31, 1967

Suggested Internship Program each United States congressman or senator has a staff of administrative assistants. I stress that while the hon. member's proposal is commendable, there is room for expanding it. In saying these words I hope I will be pardoned for advertising thereby another resolution on the order paper in my own name, which I hope will come before the house soon.
My own proposal is to provide members of parliament with administrative assistants who would help them to do research and to communicate with officials. Though I support the hon. member's proposal, its weakness is that it is aimed at helping the students and professors involved, more than members of parliament. It is important for our students to know more of our parliamentary system; there is a serious need to inform the Canadian public about its workings. They all should have greater factual knowledge of the workings of this system. Not enough of the people teaching political science in our universities possess the type of first hand knowledge that the hon. member suggests would flow from his proposal. Our professors and students do not have the first hand knowledge that hon. members have; it is vital that more people become intimately aware of the workings of our parliamentary and political system. In that regard, certainly, an internship program is useful and necessary, but if there is any priority, it is to help members of parliament perform their work rather than to help students and professors to learn more about parliament. Primarily, our aim ought to be to help members of parliament carry out their duties to the Canadian public more effectively.
Hon. members ought to have assistants who will keep in touch with government officials, follow up correspondence and requests, help in the preparation of committee work and in work to be performed in the house, gather information, carry out research and so on. When an hon. member is in the house or in committee he cannot deal with officials with respect to matters of policy which concern his area or the country at large; he cannot discuss with officials or ministers problems concerning his riding or the country at large; he cannot discuss with members of the public those problems which they feel he ought to deal with. A member of parliament needs someone whose main efforts are directed toward helping him perform a better job. This is more important to provide training for students, useful though that may be.


If there are difficulties with the hon. member's proposal I submit they would disappear were there added to it a broader, general scheme to provide full time administrative assistants for members of parliament. The hon. member suggests that interns would work from six to nine months and then go back to the schools they came from. I think hon. members will agree that it takes approximately six months, more or less, thinking back to their own first days here as members for one to learn his way around, to know how the system works, whom to talk to and where to look-to become really useful, in other words. Were we to follow the hon. member's proposal, just when the intern is becoming useful he would return to his university or law school. There is room for a system where someone might stay for several years, so that he might put into effect the experience he has garnered in his initial period of apprenticeship. There is room for people to make careers of serving as administrative assistants to members of parliament. You will find these assistants-people who are well educated and well informed-serving congressmen and senators in the United States.
Why should the internship program be limited to students of political science, journalism and law school professors? What about students of accounting, business, or history? They might also participate in the program to good effect. I should point out, however, since I think the hon. member's proposal is sound, that I do not wish to have my remarks taken in a negative, critical sense.
The hon. member's proposal therefore ought to be broadened to make eligible categories of graduate studies other than he has mentioned. However, with a broader system of providing administrative assistants hon. members could have people working with them who have completed their education and have experience in wider fields, in addition to those mentioned in the notice of motion. Under a general system such as I have mentioned one ought to be able to recruit assistants from fields of endeavour other than the law and political science. What about accounting, business, the labour movement, and other areas of activity?
Were my proposal adopted, each member could have an assistant or assistants. However, hon. members representing ridings with smaller population, say, might possibly share an administrative assistant. In the initial period of the program, an assistant might be used by several members.
May 31, 1967

It is important also to ensure that the intern or assistant has a political philosophy and policy aims that are compatible with those of the member he serves, or else stresses and strains might be set up which would not help the member or the intern. Basically, the intern and the member he serves should have the same political philosophies and aims. That would be a positive feature of a general scheme of permitting members of parliament to have administrative assistance over and above the hon. member's proposal.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
There is certainly room for the proposal of the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) but I suggest priority should be given to a general scheme for providing administrative assistance to members of parliament along the lines I have outlined. If my proposal is not given priority, then at least the two proposals should be handled together. I fear that if the hon. member's proposal were dealt with first of all it would strenghthen the hands of those who do not fully understand the need for a modern parliamentary system to deal effectively with the complexities of present-day government.
My own view is that this is a constructive proposal, but that the implementation of a general scheme should be given priority. The public does not sufficiently realize that we in this parliament have ultimately to take responsibility for the operation of a government apparatus employing some 300,000 people, including those in crown corporations, and handling a budget of some $11 billions.
In these circumstances members of parliament need assistants working directly with them and responsible to them-people who are outside the government apparatus-so as to help members find out what is going on and inform themselves and the public about the details and the operation of the system. Armed with this knowledge members would be in a position to influence more effectively than is possible at the present time the direction which this apparatus is taking.
The impression is sometimes conveyed that all the work of parliament is done only in the House of Commons, or perhaps in the house and Senate. Useful as it may be as a forum for speaking to the nation and placing the views of members on the record, useful as it may be for taking broad, formal decisions, this house is really not a place for carrying out on a day to day basis the real work of
Suggested Internship Program overseeing the operations of a modern government and achieving legislative oversight in a meaningful way. It is therefore in the public interest that elected representatives of the public should be given the facilities to do the job expected of them.
It will become increasingly likely that what we are doing may well give the appearance of supervising the work of the government of our country, but will be far from the reality. We may well be doing nothing more than going through the motions, rather than dealing with the true substance of government.
The lack of staff to which the hon. member and I have alluded, and which had led us to place our respective notices of motion on the order paper, limits the degree of supervision over legislation which ought to be exercised by the representatives of the Canadian people in the interests of those they serve. Those who send us here expect us to perform this task and are surprised to find we lack the facilities to enable us to carry out all the responsibilities which should be carried out on their behalf.
In conclusion, let me once more commend the hon. member for having placed this resolution on the order paper, permitting us to air our views on this subject once again. Though it may not seem to affect the public as directly as some of the other matters we deal with -economic development and social welfare measures, for example-in the long run it may well turn out to be as important as any of these things if we are to make sure that long after this centennial year is over we shall continue to have a government which is really responsive to the demands and needs of the people of Canada.

At least this would start the ball rolling.
There is one thing such a proposal could do. It could provide a means of avoiding the excessive cost which arises in the United States Senate in connection with secretaries and assistants to senators. We in Canada could not undertake that kind of expenditure.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly concur with the principle enunciated in this motion and would agree that the young intelligentsia of this country should be exposed to the practical workings of our national legislative process. However, the actual wording of the motion seems to indicate that most of the benefit would accrue to the young people involved. This of course has some merit. I believe it would give these young gentlemen a clearer concept of parliament and of the duties and responsibilities of members of parliament, and if this were so I believe we might get a great deal more sympathy.
The type of individual who could be expected to participate in an internship program is likely to be one who would later have a great deal of influence upon public opinion, and later on through public utterances and editorials he would be able to project a much more objective and salutary image of parliament itself.
The other advantage of this type of program, as I see it, is the fact that these young gentlemen would become acquainted with members of parliament. This could be bad or good. After a short time in parliament perhaps they might think it would not be a bad idea to run for public office. Of course it
May 31. 1967	COMMONS
could be a two-edged sword: They might decide never to catch the political disease.
Civic groups and many public spirited citizens have stridently deplored the lack of our young people going into public life, and the apathy of the general public. This is a valid fear. We all recognize the ingredients of a healthy, vital, and progressive democratic process. What is needed is a veritable array of dedicated young men willing to enter public life, ready and able to make the sacrifices that it demands. If we are to preserve and enhance our parliamentary system we must have this type of individual. Therefore if this plan awakens to even a small extent a feeling for politics in the young people involved, then for that reason alone the plan is justified. However, the real merit of the plan is the assistance it would give to members of parliament.
What about the plight of the ordinary member, and in particular I refer to the backbencher? I have been in this house one and a half years, and frankly I feel the great majority of members are hard working. They are trying to do their best for their ridings and for the country, but I believe members should have more time to ponder the great issues of the day, to study legislation, and to analyse briefs. This cannot be done if their time is consumed with committee work and answering correspondence.
At present we have fine offices. We have secretaries. We have very adequate equipment, but what we need is some assistance so far as the administration of our offices is concerned. I do not believe we should have an assistant for each member. I think at first this would not be acceptable, but we could have a pool of assistants, and members wanting to use them could use them. This is not a plan to hire people to do our legitimate work. It is a plan to make members more productive; and if we are more productive, then the country as a whole benefits. I believe this plan should be tried, and if it does not work it can be discarded.
It is an old axiom that the ordinary member is here merely to vote and look after his riding. This indictment is only partially true. I submit that ordinary members can be very influential concerning government policy. I believe they could participate in the debates in this chamber to a greater extent than at present. They can participate in caucus and on committees. They can participate in debates during private members hour.

Under the present system, however, I believe the private members hour to be a Model T in the jet age. We are supposed to have five hours for private members business each week. This is fine in theory, but the time in practice is reduced drastically. It is reduced during the budget debate, during supply debate, and during debate on the speech from the throne. At present, private members resolutions occupy two hours each week, and this leaves only one hour a week on Friday afternoon for private members public bills. I believe that private bills which deal chiefly with corporation matters should be eliminated from the private members hour. They have no place in the House of Commons.
We were able to eliminate divorce bills from the private members hour, and this was a very salutary step. They are now handled much more expeditiously in the Senate and everybody is quite relieved. The next logical step should be to transfer all private bills out of the house to some department such as the Department of the Secretary of State. In this way the applicant would receive a better and more prompt hearing, and there would be more time for private members business in this house.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Sometimes the whole concept of the private members hour is queried. Sometimes it is suggested that we do not need it at all. I think we need it, and for many reasons. The first basic reason is that it gives every member an opportunity to speak in this house, and that is something that is not easy to do. It is a rather intimidating place.
In the first place, all the members of this house travel across the country. They become acquainted with the needs, aspirations and feelings of the people of this land. They can interpret the mood and the temper of this nation. Of course, some of the bills which are presented are neither logical nor well thought out. Some of the ideas are good, some are bad, and some of them are indifferent; but at least the attitudes of this nation are crystallized and held up to public debate and scrutiny. I think this is a very fine thing.
The two reasons which have been advanced for the retention of the private members hour are to a certain extent most helpful, but the basic reason I believe is that it can be used as a vehicle to translate these ideas into legislation. At the present time about 100 per cent of the bills are talked out. They literally die, without having the remotest chance of being passed. I believe this is wrong. In my view

Suggested Internship Program every bill should be voted upon before six o'clock. If it were accepted, then it could be sent to a committee for examination. If it should have merit, then it could be referred back to the house for possible legislation. This would enhance the role of the private member. This is what we are interested in.
This motion refers to parliamentary reform. I spoke on this subject previously. Because of antiquated procedures the average person has a very poor concept of parliament. In the eyes of the people, we are bumbling, ineffective and impotent; we are paralysed by stifling time consuming procedures. The danger in this attitude is very evident.
